item.title: Retraction of a liquid drop in a Hele-Shaw cell
item.description: arXiv:2610.19056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a long liquid drop is confined in a Hele-Shaw cell, the pull of surface tension produces a rapid retraction of its tip, causing it to bulge out as it draws up the excess liquid. Using numerical simulations, we demonstrate that this retraction is self-similar at long times, with the speed of retraction slowing like $t^{-1/2}$, where $t$ is the duration of retraction. After showing how this scaling can be understood using force and mass balance, we perform an asymptotic analysis of the Hele-Shaw equations to derive both the shape of the retracting drop, as well as prefactors of the scaling laws. Excellent agreement is found between our simulations and theory, and the experimental consequences are pointed out.
item.dc:creator: Luke Neville, Paul R. Kaneelil

item.title: Two-Way Coupled Dynamics of Quantized Vortex Bundle Formation in Spatially Periodic Normal-Fluid Turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.19577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using fully coupled two-way simulations combining the vortex filament model with the Navier--Stokes equations, we discover that quantized vortices in superfluid $^4$He are systematically rolled up into coherent bundles within normal-fluid vortex tubes. Although co-rotating quantized vortices do not aggregate spontaneously, mutual friction with the normal fluid actively drives their bundling, directly inheriting the spatial hierarchy of classical turbulence. Mutual friction excites high-wavenumber normal-fluid vortex tubes adjacent to quantized vortices, while the superfluid forms a nested structure of thick low-wavenumber outer tubes and fine high-wavenumber inner tubes around the vortex lines. A distinct time lag between superfluid kinetic energy and dissipation fuels the energy cascade, giving rise to Kolmogorov's $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum. Crucially, bundle lifetimes are governed by the ratio of the local coupling time scale $t_\mathrm{cl}$ to the Kolmogorov dissipation time scale $\tau_\eta$ ($t_\mathrm{cl}/\tau_\eta < 20$), leading to enhanced thermal stability at higher temperatures. These findings establish a unified mechanism for two-fluid multiscale vortex organization.
item.dc:creator: Hiromichi Kobayashi, Makoto Tsubota, Rio Yokota

item.title: Response of Confined Mesoscale Flames to Acoustic Forcing
item.description: arXiv:2610.19661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mesoscale combustion plays a vital role in applications ranging from portable power generation to micro-propulsion systems. This study investigates the response of mesoscale flames to upstream acoustic forcing across three characteristic flame regimes: Flames with Repetitive Extinction and Ignition (FREI), Stable Flames (SF), and Propagating Flames (PF). Acoustic forcing is applied over a broad range of pressure intensities at the first harmonic of the combustor tube. At low forcing intensities, all the flame regimes exhibit oscillations at the forcing frequency without qualitative changes in their respective flame behaviours. However, as the acoustic pressure increases, all flame regimes transition to a common unsteady regime characterised by periodic ignition-extinction cycles (resembling FREI) alongside strong oscillations at the forcing frequency. This response is identified as the oscillating FREI (O-FREI) regime, in which increasing forcing intensity leads to a reduction in the mean heat release rate, an amplification of oscillations at the forcing frequency, and a drop in the Strouhal number associated with the ignition-extinction cycle. The response characteristics across all flame regimes are examined in detail and are further complemented using reduced-order mathematical models.
item.dc:creator: Akhil Aravind, Balasundaram Mohan, Saptarshi Basu

item.title: Extreme-Scale Super-Resolution of Homogeneous Turbulence from a Single Realization
item.description: arXiv:2610.20305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Homogeneous turbulent flows exhibit recurring multiscale structures across spatially separated regions, suggesting that a single flow realization may contain sufficient information to learn representations of unresolved scales. We investigate this hypothesis through an extreme super-resolution framework in which a wide-activation deep super-resolution (WDSR) network is trained exclusively on overlapping patches extracted from a single high-resolution turbulent realization. Previously unseen flow fields are reconstructed through patchwise prediction followed by Hann-window-weighted overlap-add assembly. The framework is evaluated for two-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence at super-resolution factors of x32 and x64, representing severe spatial under-resolution. Despite the limited training data, the proposed approach reconstructs coherent vortical structures and recovers fine-scale features more accurately than conventional interpolation. Spectral and statistical analyses further demonstrate improved recovery of high-wavenumber energy content and multiscale flow characteristics. To assess the effectiveness of exploiting internal spatial information, we compare the proposed framework against WDSR models trained on 1, 25, 50, and 100 complete high-resolution snapshots without patch extraction. This comparison distinguishes the benefits of localized learning from those associated with increasing the number of training realizations. The results demonstrate that exploiting spatial redundancy within a single turbulent realization enables accurate reconstruction of previously unseen flow fields, even under extreme spatial under-resolution. These findings establish single-realization patch-based learning as a promising data-efficient approach for turbulent super-resolution when high-resolution training data are scarce.
item.dc:creator: Arth Sojitra, Muhammad Abid, Omer San

item.title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient
item.description: arXiv:2610.20372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The adverse-pressure-gradient (APG) effect challenges the classical scaling of turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) over a flat plate, and it remains unclear whether outer-layer similarity holds across a wide range of APG strengths.We assemble a benchmark comprising the present direct numerical simulation of a suction--blowing-induced separation bubble and published profiles, spanning Clauser parameters $\beta_e=0.04$--$180$ and Reynolds numbers $Re_\theta=530$--$19000$. Across this broad $(\beta_e,Re_\theta)$ parameter range, existing APG normalizations do not simultaneously collapse the two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components, leaving open whether outer similarity persists. Instead of defining new scalings, we normalize each quantity by its value at a common location $y_s$. Results are shown using $y_s=0.5\delta$, beyond the outer stress peaks. For each of the six quantities, the normalized profiles exhibit a common outer shape across the conditions, with collapse emerging for $y/\delta\gtrsim0.2$ for the velocity defects and $y/\delta\gtrsim0.4$ for the Reynolds stresses. The collapse-error analysis shows that outer self-similarity is retained over a broad range of $y_s$ within the outer region and is not restricted to $y_s=0.5\delta$. Furthermore, explicit expressions are provided for the normalized outer profiles. These results support component-wise outer similarity under strong APGs and provide compact references for APG turbulence-model assessment and conditional profile reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Xuan Shi, Mingze Ma, Xi Chen

item.title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation
item.description: arXiv:2610.20470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lab-scale membrane distillation (MD) modules are commonly used for membrane characterization and developing empirical heat-transfer correlations. Entrance-induced flow structures can introduce geometry-specific effects into measured temperature polarization (TP) and heat transfer. However, the dependence of these effects on module geometry and flow condition remains unclear. We performed three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) over inlet Reynolds numbers of $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}=10$-$1000$, focusing on side-chamber length and main-channel height. We discovered that counter-rotating streamwise vortices formed near the main-channel entrance across all geometries, but their downstream persistence increased with $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. At lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$, the vortices mostly decayed before mid-channel, while at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ they persisted farther downstream and produced pronounced spatial variations in TP. Increasing side-chamber length reduced the secondary-flow kinetic energy entering the main channel, and generally strengthened TP, whereas increasing main-channel height reduced the bulk velocity and streamwise kinetic energy, resulting in a thicker thermal boundary layer and stronger TP. For most geometries, the deviation from the straight-channel baseline changed from stronger TP at lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ to weaker TP at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. Entrance effects therefore vary in both magnitude and direction with operating condition and cannot be represented by a constant correction across the Reynolds-number range.
item.dc:creator: Soyoung Kim, Tiezheng Tong, Yinuo Noah Yao

item.title: A Multi-frame Analysis of Flow Reversal in Tidal Bore
item.description: arXiv:2610.18913v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A tidal bore is a nonlinear step like surge propagating on the top of a river counter-current. The scientific literature reports that the passage of the tidal front may induce local flow reversals and, in some cases, a global reversal of the river current. Here, combining Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) measurements and 2D numerical simulations based on a Weakly Compressible Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (WCSPH) method, we show that the flow classification of tidal bores must explicitly take into account the frame of reference. When the river flow does not reverse after the bore passing, this is a consequence of the perspective imposed by the background current (itself resulting from the previous tide and the natural river discharge toward the sea). Depending on the relative magnitudes of the river current and the velocity field induced by the bore, one may observe a global reversal, a local reversal (or both), or no reversal at all. When the tide is spatially inhomogeneous, with a tidal range that varies along the estuary rather than a simple step in water depth, transitions between bore types may occur during the bore passing.
item.dc:creator: Assia Belemkadem (PPrime), Johan Fourdrinoy (PPrime), Anthony Beaudoin (PPrime), Germain Rousseaux (PPrime)

item.title: A Unified Framework for Bell-Shaped Gaussian Quadratures in Deterministic Boltzmann Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2610.18931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework that constructs Bell-shaped Gaussian quadratures for deterministic Boltzmann solvers. The proposed framework establishes a general class of bell-shaped weight functions together with the corresponding integral transformations, revealing the common mathematical structure underlying existing generalized Gaussian quadratures. Based on this framework, a unified procedure for constructing discrete velocity sets is developed by combining radial quadratures with appropriate directional quadratures in different velocity-space dimensions. Several existing generalized Gaussian quadratures are naturally recovered as special cases, while the proposed framework provides a systematic route for constructing new quadrature rules based on different bell-shaped weight functions. Extensive benchmark simulations over a broad range of flow regimes demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves high integration accuracy and computational efficiency with significantly fewer discrete velocities than conventional quadrature strategies. Overall, the proposed framework not only unifies existing generalized Gaussian quadratures under a common mathematical foundation but also establishes a general design principle for the systematic development of efficient velocity-space quadratures in deterministic Boltzmann solvers.
item.dc:creator: Shanshan Dong, Lu Wang, Guanqing Wang

item.title: Kinetic Equations and Turbulence in Large $N$ Vector and SYK-like Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.19130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We apply large $N$ expansion techniques to derive kinetic equations for strongly coupled, far-from-equilibrium field theories with $O(N)$ symmetry. For large $N$ vector models, the quasi-classical approximation holds. Incorporating arbitrary momentum-dependent interactions, we show the dynamics obey the standard kinetic equation, with the scattering amplitude given by the retarded propagator of the auxiliary Hubbard-Stratonovich field. This has broad applications to systems like spin wave and Langmuir ion-acoustic turbulence. For large $N$ random coupling (SYK-like) models in $d$ dimensions, leading-order melon diagrams induce order-one propagator renormalization and finite spectral width. The corresponding kinetic equation, unlike those for standard weakly interacting systems, does not have a local-in-time collision integral. We find evidence for a stationary, scale-invariant infrared solution, revealing a potentially novel strong turbulence scaling exponent.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Rosenhaus, Daniel Schubring

item.title: GeONet: Geometry-Encoded Operator Network for Predicting Flow in Heterogeneous Porous Media
item.description: arXiv:2610.19493v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rapid prediction of pressure-driven flow in microfluidic porous media is important for experimental design, tracer-test interpretation, and digital-twin development for subsurface energy and critical mineral applications. High-fidelity simulations resolve geometry-controlled flow but are computationally expensive across large geometry ensembles. Here, we introduce GeONet, a Geometry-Encoded Operator Network that predicts steady-state pressure fields by jointly representing material properties, spatial coordinates, and solid--void geometry. GeONet extends the Branch--Trunk architecture with a dedicated Leaf Network encoding the binary domain mask through multiscale features. The Branch Network represents porosity and permeability, the Trunk Network combines coordinates with local geometric descriptors and random Fourier features, and a gated DeepMixer integrates these representations to predict pressure. GeONet was trained and evaluated using 5,000 PFLOTRAN simulations of heterogeneous Reduced Complexity Platform domains, comprising nearly 30 TB of data. Comparisons with pore-scale Stokes solutions across three geometries yielded Pearson correlations of 0.987--0.991 and $R^2$ values of 0.974--0.982, supporting PFLOTRAN as reference data. Under matched partitions and two-stage hyperparameter optimization, GeONet substantially outperformed a boundary-condition-aware DeepONet baseline. Across three held-out domains, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0381--0.0500, MAPE of 1.76--2.59%, and $R^2$ of 0.9673--0.9822, versus 0.1483--0.2040, 7.81--10.45%, and 0.5658--0.7126 for DeepONet, respectively. On three additional unseen geometries, GeONet achieved NRMSE of 0.0448--0.0676 and $R^2$ of 0.9511--0.9770. These results demonstrate improved accuracy, pressure-range preservation, and cross-geometry generalization through explicit geometry encoding.
item.dc:creator: Md Lal Mamud, Maruti K. Mudunuru, Yucheng Fu, Aramy Troung, Satish Karra, Ivani Patel, Arunima Bhattacharjee, Tamas Varga, Pratanu Roy, Michael Penwarden, Rajesh K. Singh, Arjun Chakrawal, Kalyana B. Nakshatrala, Christof Meile, Erin Rooney, Glenn Hammond

item.title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles
item.description: arXiv:2610.19631v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Active flows are often confined by soft, deformable boundaries that they can push against, reshape, and in turn get reorganized by. Motivated by this interplay, we combine theory and numerical simulations to analyze the morphodynamics of an elastic vesicle enclosing a dilute suspension of extensile active particles. We model the two-dimensional vesicle as a weakly extensible elastic ring with bending rigidity, immersed in a Stokesian fluid, and describe the confined active suspension using a kinetic theory. The vesicle and the suspension are coupled hydrodynamically, through the kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the interface, and energetically, through a single alignment interaction that simultaneously aligns active particles with the membrane and the membrane with the particles. We show that this interaction reduces to a weak-anchoring boundary condition familiar from passive liquid crystals and derive a closed-form quiescent equilibrium state in which the nematic order in the suspension organizes into a vortex with a +1 defect core. A stability analysis of this state predicts an ordered hierarchy of activity thresholds at which successive shape modes of the vesicle are destabilized, as well as a purely passive, anchoring-driven instability of floppy vesicles. Nonlinear simulations, performed with a volume-conserving immersed boundary method, reveal that each threshold crossing gives rise to a distinct emergent state: a static spindle with boundary-pinned defects, a rotor that tank treads against its own rotation, a fluctuating spinner, and a turbulent state in which the vesicle acts as a self-stirring compartment. Beyond demonstrating how boundary deformability sculpts, and is sculpted by, confined active matter, our results open the door to study hydrodynamic interactions between such active vesicles and to use membrane fluctuations as a probe of activity of suspensions.
item.dc:creator: Devadevan M M, Brato Chakrabarti

item.title: eMOOD: Entropy-Based Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection for High-Order Shock-Capturing Finite-Volume Schemes
item.description: arXiv:2610.20133v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present eMOOD, an entropy-guided evolution of the Multidimensional Optimal Order Detection (MOOD) framework for high-order finite-volume methods on unstructured meshes. A novel troubled-cell indicator based on numerical entropy production replaces the classical relaxed discrete maximum principle. Using entropy generation as a physically motivated measure of non-smoothness, the detector targets shocks, contact discontinuities and under-resolved flow features with a compact stencil. Compared with conventional MOOD detection, eMOOD reduces flagged cells by up to 75%, improving efficiency and reducing memory-access overhead. The detector is used within both the classical MOOD cascade of progressively reduced-order schemes and a novel MOOD-CWENO hybrid, which retains inexpensive linear reconstruction in smooth regions and activates nonlinear high-order reconstruction only where needed. Implemented in the open-source parallel solver UCNS3D, the methodology is assessed on the Shu-Osher shock-entropy-wave interaction, double Mach reflection, supersonic forward-facing step, shock-helium-bubble interaction and triple material point problems. These benchmarks encompass strong shock interactions, shock-induced instabilities, multi-material interfaces and vortex-dominated flows, testing robustness, shock capturing and accuracy on unstructured meshes. Results show that eMOOD preserves the accuracy and robustness of reference CWENO and MOOD formulations while achieving speed-ups of up to 20% without loss of solution quality. Its compact detection stencil, reduced memory footprint and improved localisation offer a more scalable and efficient framework for massively parallel high-order compressible-flow simulations. item.title: High-Frequency Mass Transfer Enabling Over-Limiting Currents in Porous Electrodes
item.description: arXiv:2610.20211v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classical film theory predicts a finite diffusion-limited current at porous electrodes. However, over-limiting currents (OLCs), which exceed this limit, are often observed and have been attributed to surface charge, confinement, or electrokinetic effects. Here, we use a frequency-domain framework to identify a different mechanism governed by the time scale of concentration variation. For perfectly reactive interfaces, the spectral Sherwood number, a frequency-dependent dimensionless measure of interfacial mass transfer relative to molecular diffusion, grows as $\Shnd\sim\omega^{1/2}$ at high frequency, while its phase approaches $\pi/4$. This response corresponds to the semi-infinite Warburg limit of the electrochemical impedance. A scaling analysis shows that the exponent and prefactor are determined by diffusion within a thin layer adjacent to the interface and are therefore independent of the global pore geometry. Numerical results for parallel plates, circular tubes, and twelve porous microstructures confirm this scaling. Geometry, flow strength, and flow direction affect the low-frequency response and crossover frequency, but not the asymptotic scaling in the high-frequency limit. This temporal route to OLCs requires neither surface charge nor confinement and could inform the design of systems for pulsed electrodeposition, mineral recovery and renewable-energy storage.
item.dc:creator: Md Abdul Hamid, Kyle C. Smith

item.title: An Omni-Temporal Framework for Hydrodynamic Dispersion and Reaction in Porous Media
item.description: arXiv:2505.06063v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many applications involve porous-media transport driven on time scales comparable to the pore-scale diffusion time, for which classical pseudo-steady dispersion models based on time-invariant transport coefficients may become inaccurate. While frequency-dependent dispersion has been studied in non-reactive porous media, a corresponding framework that simultaneously accounts for advection, diffusion, and heterogeneous interfacial reaction remains lacking. We address this gap by introducing an omni-temporal framework based on volume averaging of the frequency-domain pore-scale advection-diffusion equation subject to a Robin boundary condition spanning the full range of interfacial reactivity. The resulting upscaled formulation yields four frequency-dependent transfer functions: a dispersion tensor, an advection-suppression vector, a spectral Sherwood number, and a reactivity-bias vector, with the reactivity-bias vector introduced here for the first time. Analytical solutions for fully developed flow between parallel plates and through circular tubes reveal distinct kinetics- and diffusion-limited regimes, including capacitive and semi-infinite Warburg-type frequency responses. Comparisons of transient breakthrough curves with direct numerical simulations demonstrate substantial improvement over conventional pseudo-steady dispersion, particularly for short-duration pulses. Application to a periodic array of square rods under cross flow further demonstrates the frameworks applicability beyond canonical geometries.
item.dc:creator: Md Abdul Hamid, Kyle C. Smith

item.title: Comparative Numerical Study of Film Cooling Strategies for Thermal Protection of a Kerosene-Fueled Oblique Detonation Combustor
item.description: arXiv:2605.05874v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Thermal protection remains a major challenge for oblique detonation engines (ODEs), whose combustors combine intense heat release, anchored on oblique detonation waves (ODWs). This study numerically investigates the effects of coolant type and mass flow rate on the flow structure, thermal environment and propulsion performance of a film-cooled kerosene-air ODE combustor at Mach 10 and 15 km altitude. Three active cooling strategies are compared under identical conditions: air film cooling, gaseous-kerosene film cooling, and liquid-kerosene mist cooling. Stable, wall-attached oblique-detonation propagation and the canonical wave structure are maintained, with the wave-coolant interaction depending systematically on the coolant medium. Air injection causes the greatest disturbance to the initiation region and downstream wave interactions, yielding the largest propulsion penalty. The cooling strategies substantially reduce the near-wall thermal load but produce distinct wall-temperature distributions. Gaseous-kerosene cooling yields a spatially periodic response from the discrete injection slots, whereas liquid-kerosene mist cooling gives a smoother and lower near-wall temperature through two-phase mixing and phase-change heat absorption. Liquid-kerosene mist cooling provides the most favorable balance between thermal protection and propulsion performance at low to moderate injection levels. With further increases in injection level, the thermal benefit approaches saturation while the propulsion penalty continues to grow: the mean near-wall fluid temperature reduction remains about 87% across both the inter-slot and cooling-slot wall segments, whereas the total specific impulse is reduced by about 3%-5%. These results quantify the thermal-propulsive trade-off across film-cooling media and demonstrate the potential of fuel-based cooling for thermal management in hypersonic ODE combustors.
item.dc:creator: Jianghong Li, Songbai Yao, Wenwu Zhang

item.title: Interfacial waves from pressure forcing: role of the transients
item.description: arXiv:2605.12254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A localised overpressure translating at a uniform speed greater than a critical value acts at the interface between two deep fluid layers with different densities. We analyse the resulting wave patterns using an initial-value problem formulation within the linearised, inviscid, potential flow framework. The steady-state interface exhibits short capillary waves ahead of the forcing and long gravity waves behind it, arising from an asymmetric cancellation of Fourier components in the far field. The time-dependent part of the solution, decaying algebraically with time, plays a crucial role in this mechanism. This contrasts with classical steady approaches, which require additional conditions to select a unique solution. We extend this approach to a two-fluid interface and validate the predictions against nonlinear simulations.
item.dc:creator: Vinod Kumar Kadari, Nikhil Yewale, Palas Kumar Farsoiya, Y. S. Mayya, Ratul Dasgupta

item.title: Experimental observations of sub-threshold triadic resonances in internal wave beams
item.description: arXiv:2609.26689v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work examines sub-threshold triadic responses to a vortex-ring-induced perturbation of an internal gravity-wave field, using sparsity-promoting dynamic mode decomposition (spDMD) to diagnose wave structures from experimental observations. Compared with a standard approach to dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) that selects modes by truncation of the singular value spectrum, spDMD, an alternative approach that instead seeks to minimise reconstruction error, is shown here to robustly identify previously indistinguishable oscillatory signals of high frequency in cases of both triadic resonance instability (TRI) and sub-threshold sustained triadic response (STR). These signals are consistent with wave--wave interaction products composed of a primary internal wave with frequency $\omega_0$, and secondary TRI waves with frequencies $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ respectively, leading to signals with frequencies $\omega_3 = \omega_0 + \omega_1$ and $\omega_4 = \omega_0 + \omega_2$. We show that these signals satisfy conditions for resonance, but fail to satisfy the dispersion relation for internal waves, indicating that they are confined, non-propagating oscillatory signals rather than freely propagating internal waves. A hierarchical analysis of wave--wave interactions provides evidence that feedback between both branches of the TRI secondary waves gives rise to these signals. Whilst we expect our observations to generalise to many classes of wave--wave interaction, we cannot exclude the possibility that the particular observations we make in the laboratory may arise due to reflections of the primary wave from a free surface. However, beneath strongly density-stratified regions of the ocean we would expect to find these interaction pathways faced with the same geometric configuration, so we are confident our findings will transfer directly to the natural environment.
item.dc:creator: Laura J. Irvine, Katherine M. Grayson, Andrew G. W. Lawrie, Stuart B. Dalziel

item.title: High-level, efficient ocean modeling at all scales with Oceananigans
item.description: arXiv:2502.14148v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We describe the user interface, governing equations, and numerical methods underpinning the ocean modeling software called "Oceananigans". Oceananigans development has been led by the Climate Modeling Alliance as part of a larger effort to build a trainable climate model with quantifiable uncertainty. Notably, Oceananigans is written in the Julia programming language, is optimized for GPUs, and can efficiently simulate all scales of ocean motion ranging from millimeter-scale turbulence in a small box to planetary-scale ocean circulation. We argue that this combination of capabilities is enabled by a design that combines a basic, easy-to-optimize, GPU-friendly structured finite volume algorithm exposed behind a high-level, programmable user interface. This design negotiates a dual mandate for highest-possible performance (to support state-of-the-art applications) and enhanced accessibility (to facilitate adoption and development). The dual mandate aims ultimately to accelerate the progress of Earth system science.
item.dc:creator: Gregory L. Wagner, Simone Silvestri, Navid C. Constantinou, Ali Ramadhan, Jean-Michel Campin, Chris Hill, Tomas Chor, Jago Strong-Wright, Xin Kai Lee, Francis Poulin, Andre Souza, Keaton J. Burns, Siddhartha Bishnu, John Marshall, Raffaele Ferrari

item.title: Homothetic Self-Similar Solutions to the Incompressible Navier-Stokes Equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.12159v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate homothetic forward self-similar solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations: the solutions $\overline{U}$ for which both $\overline{U}$ and $\beta \overline{U}$ are self-similar profiles for some nontrivial $\beta$. Homothetic solutions are, in addition, the only solutions for which a singular limit argument can be used to prove non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf solutions along the lines of the Jia-\v{S}ver\'{a}k program. In three dimensions, and for sufficiently regular initial data, we prove a Liouville theorem that rules out the existence of non-trivial homothetic solutions. In two dimensions, our Liouville theorem reproves a result of Luo and Shvydkoy that the only decaying homothetic solution with continuous angular data is the Oseen vortex. In addition, we prove that the Euler equations linearized around the Oseen vortex are stable in some subspaces of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$, for example in the space of $2$-fold rotationally symmetric functions. On the other hand, we also discover a homothetic solution for which an unstable approximate eigenvalue of the linearized Euler equations exists.
item.dc:creator: Tim Binz, Matei P. Coiculescu
